'''''Succisa pratensis''''', known as '''devil's-bit scabious''' or simply '''devil's-bit''', is a [[flowering plant]] in the honeysuckle family [[Caprifoliaceae]], formerly included in the teasel family [[Dipsacaceae]]. It is common throughout northern Europe and western Asia in heathland, unimproved damp grassland and chalk or limestone grassland, where it is restricted to nutrient-poor soils. It has decreased somewhat due to agricultural intensification in many areas, but remains widespread and even common throughout its range. Its name derives from the curiously truncated root, which in ancient times was thought to be associated with magical or medicinal properties.

==Description==
[[File:Succisa pratensis premorse.jpg|thumb|left|The root of a mature devil's-bit scabious, showing the premorse (bitten-off) taproot.]]
Devil's-bit scabious is a [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[herbaceous]] plant, sometimes growing to 1 m (3 ft) or more tall but often much smaller, for example just a few centimetres in montane heathland or Scottish [[machair]].<ref name="Evans">{{Cite book |last=Evans |first=P.A. |title=Flora of Assynt |last2=Evans |first2=I.M. |last3=Rothero |first3=G.P. |publisher=P.A. & I.M. Evans |year=2002 |isbn=0-9541813-0-1}}</ref> The stem is erect to ascending, often somewhat arched, roughly hairy and unbranched. The leaves are arranged in opposite pairs, the basal ones being 2-15 cm (exceptionally up to 30 cm) long, ovate and sometimes slightly toothed; the stem leaves being smaller and narrower, [[lanceolate]],  [https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/connate connate], and shortly sheathing around the stem. All the leaves have winged [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] up to 2 cm long and are also roughly hairy.<ref name="Stace-2010">{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles|url=https://archive.org/details/newflorabritishi00stac|url-access=limited|edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location = Cambridge, U.K.| page=[https://archive.org/details/newflorabritishi00stac/page/n831 796]|isbn=9780521707725}}</ref> A curious feature of this plant is the taproot, which grows to about 5 mm thickness in its first year and then becomes woody and dies away at the tip, leaving a [https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/premorse premorse] stump that produces shallower-growing lateral roots in the second year.<ref name="Grieve-1931">{{cite book |last1=Grieve |first1=Maud |title=A Modern Herbal |date=1931 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0-486-22798-7}}</ref><ref name="Sell-2006">{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 4 |date=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>
[[File:Succisa pratensis stem leaves.jpg|thumb|The leaves are connate and shortly sheathing around the stem.]]
[[File:Succisa pratensis roots.jpg|thumb|First year plants have a full-length taproot.]]

Inflorescences are either terminal or in the leaf axils and consist of one, three or sometimes more [[Pseudanthium|compound flower heads]] or capitula, each of which contain 30-50 bluish to violet (occasionally pink or white) flowers in a tightly-packed, almost hemispherical dome 15-25 mm across. Below the flowerhead there are two rows of green involucral bracts up to 10 mm long. The receptacle is up to 10 mm across and slightly elongated. Within the flowerhead there are numerous ciliate bracts and as many flowers, which are made up of an epicalyx or "involucel" which is formed from 4 fused bracteoles, a calyx tube with 4 lobes terminated by 4-5 black bristles, and a corolla up to 7 mm long, also with 4 lobes. All the flowers are similar as they are not divided into ray and disc florets.<ref name="Adams 1955">{{Cite journal |last=Adams |first=A.W. |title=Succisa pratensis Moench |year=1955 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2257031 |journal=Journal of Ecology |volume=43 |issue=2 |pages=709-718}}</ref><ref name=Sell-2006 />
[[File:Succisa pratensis sl13.jpg|thumb|Dissected base of a single flower(A), showing a bract (B) the epicalyx (C) and calyx (D).]]

The flowers are all bisexual (hermaphroditic), but on a proportion of flowerheads a majority of anthers may be abortive, thus creating the impression of [[gynodioecy]]. They are also [[Sequential hermaphroditism|protandrous]], which means the male parts mature first, followed by the female. This adds to the appearance of dioecy. In fact the flowers all produce 4 stamens with very long filaments and purple anthers, and one style with a cream-coloured stigma. The fruit is a small achene, about 0.5 mm long.<ref name=Sell-2006 />

==Taxonomy==
Devil's-bit scabious was not known, or at least not mentioned, by the [[Ancient Greek]] and [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] herbalists, presumably because it does not grow in those regions.<ref name=GBIF>{{Cite web |title=Succisa pratensis Moench |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/2888811 |access-date=15 October 2025 |website=Global Biodiversity Information Forum}}</ref> The earliest mention of it in literature may have been in [[Rudolf Jakob Camerarius|Camerer's]] 1586 edition of [[Pietro Andrea Mattioli]]'s herbal ''De Plantis Epitome Utilissima''. The name he gives is ''Succisa Officinis, Morsus diaboli'', which is a typical pre-Linnaean polynomial and not valid as a modern botanical name.

[[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] renamed it ''Scabiosa succisa'' in [https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/358117#page/110/mode/1up Species Plantarum, 1753], but it was returned to the genus ''Succisa'' by [[Conrad Moench]] in 1794 and renamed ''pratensis''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Moench |first=Conrad |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/7340 |title=Methodus plantas horti botanici et agri Marburgensis :a staminum situ describendi |last2=Moench |first2=Conrad |date=1794 |publisher=in officina nova libraria academiae |volume=v.2 |location=Marburgi Cattorum}}</ref> This name has been accepted ever since,  but while modern books separate the genus ''Succisa'' from ''Scabiosa'' by the number of corolla lobes, that is not the distinction that Moench made.

The scientific name comes from the Latin ''[https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/succisus#Latin succisus]'', which means cut down or truncated, while ''pratensis'' means "of the meadow". Linnaeus's name for it, ''Scabiosa'', derives from the Latin verb scabo, scabere:<ref>{{Citation |title=scabo |date=2023-11-14 |work=Wiktionary, the free dictionary |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/w/index.php?title=scabo&oldid=76654652 |access-date=2025-10-10 |language=en}}</ref> "to scratch." The "devil's-bit" name is sometimes said to refer to the devil biting off the root, or to its use in treating devil's bites, or [[scabies]].<ref name="Allen" />

There are no recorded hybrids of devil's-bit scabious,<ref name="Stace-1975">{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref> but numerous subspecies and varieties have been described. Adams (1955)<ref name="Adams 1955" /> lists several of these and reports how most of the characters are quickly lost in cultivation, which suggests that they are merely [[ecotypes]]. Some authorities still claim to recognise some regional subspecies, such as var. ''subcaulis'' <small>(Bernardin.) P.D. Sell</small> from Cornwall and the Scottish isles, and var. ''ovalis'' <small> (Ruoy) P.D. Sell</small>, which is supposed to occur only at Pixey Mead in Oxfordshire,<ref name=Sell-2006 /> but these are not widely accepted.<ref name=POWO />

Its chromosome number is 2''n'' = 20.<ref name="Stace-2010" />

==Identification==
Devil's-bit can be easily confused with [[Knautia arvensis|field scabious]], [[Centaurea scabiosa|greater knapweed]] and [[Scabiosa columbaria|small scabious]], but those plants all have enlarged ray florets and lobed leaves. [[Jasione montana|Sheep's-bit]] can resemble a small devil's-bit, but it has 5-lobed flowers and club-shaped anthers.

The white midrib allows the overwintering rosettes to be distinguished from those of [[Centaurea nigra|knapweed]].

==Distribution and status==
Devil's-bit scabious is common throughout most of the [[British Isles]], western and central Europe,<ref name="Blamey-1989">{{cite book | last1=Blamey | first1=Marjorie | last2=Grey-Wilson | first2=Christopher | title=The Illustrated Flora of Britain and Northern Europe | publisher=Hodder & Stoughton | publication-place=London [ | date=1989 | isbn=0-340-40170-2 | page=386 }}</ref> extending eastwards into central Asia, and it has been introduced to eastern North America. It occurs from sea level to high mountain pastures, growing as high as 2,400 m in Hungary.<ref name="Adams 1955" />

There has been no change in its range or distribution in Britain since the 1950s, but it is believed to have decreased in abundance and declined locally due to intensification of agriculture in the late 20th century.<ref name="Plant Atlas 2020">{{cite web | title=Devil's-bit Scabious ''Succisa pratensis'' Moench | website=Plant Atlas 2020| url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.23w | access-date=2025-08-10}}</ref><ref>{{PLANTS|id=SUPR|taxon=Succisa pratensis|access-date=4 December 2015}}</ref> In northern and western counties it is considered to be ubiquitous on all soils and at all altitudes, while in the south and east it is highly restricted to areas with suitable soils.<ref name=Evans /><ref name="Kitchener">{{Cite book |last=Kitchener |first=G.D. |title=Kent Rare Plant Register |year=2025 |url=https://archive.org/details/kent-rpr-2025}}</ref> Adams (1955) considered it to be more common on disturbed ground and ditch sides, such as [[Stone Age]] ditches at [[Avebury]] and [[Ancient Rome|Roman]] workings at [[Hadrian's Wall]].<ref name="Adams 1955" />

Although its status globally has not been assessed by the IUCN,<ref>{{Cite web |title=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251008172301/https://www.iucnredlist.org/ |archive-date=2025-10-08 |access-date=2025-10-11 |website=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species}}</ref> most countries consider devil's-bit not to be threatened and have given it a status of [[Least-concern species|LC]] (least concern).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Succisa pratensis - Moench |url=https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/169186 |access-date=2025-10-11 |website=eunis.eea.europa.eu}}</ref> In Britain its overall status is also LC,<ref name="Plant Atlas 2020" /> but in most English counties it is thought to be at least in a long-term decline.<ref name=Kitchener /><ref name=Lockton>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015|isbn=978-0-9530937-2-4}}</ref>

It is considered an [[axiophyte]] in most counties in England, Wales and Scotland.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |title=Axiophytes |url=https://bsbi.org/axiophytes}}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
Devil's-bit scabious grows in a wide variety of habitats but in many places, rather confusingly, it is restricted to highly localised areas on specific soil types. Adams (1955) listed its habitats in Britain as "deciduous woods (except beech), rides in coniferous plantations, poor pastures, fens, bogs roadsides, sea-cliffs and... sandy or marshy ground near the seashore." Despite this apparently wide range of situations, they are all nutrient-poor and reasonably open to sunlight. Thus, it may be abundant along a woodland ride but absent from the closed wood, or common in chalk downland but eliminated entirely from areas of farmland.<ref name="Adams 1955" /> Its [[Indicator value|Ellenberg values]] in Britain are L = 7, F = 7, R = 5, N = 2, and S = 0, which reflect how it favours damp, reasonably sunny places with neutral soils and very low fertility, and that it does not tolerate salt.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hill|first1=M.O.|last2=Mountford|first2=J.O.|last3=Roy|first3=D.B.|last4=Bunce|first4=R.G.H.|title=Ellenberg's indicator values for British plants. ECOFACT Volume 2. Technical Annex|date=1999|publisher=Institute of Terrestrial Ecology|isbn=1870393481|url=http://nora.nerc.ac.uk/6411/1/ECOFACT2a.pdf}}</ref>

The flowers are visited by various types of insects, but especially frequently by [[hoverfly|hoverflies]] of the genus ''[[Eristalis]]''.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1111/plb.12328| title = Competition for pollinators and intra-communal spectral dissimilarity of flowers| journal = Plant Biology| pages = 56–62| year = 2015| last1 = Van Der Kooi | first1 = C. J.| last2 = Pen | first2 = I.| last3 = Staal | first3 = M.| last4 = Stavenga | first4 = D. G.| last5 = Elzenga | first5 = J. T. M.| url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/273158762 | pmid=25754608 | volume=18| issue = 1| hdl = 11370/caee8d0d-9724-4056-9d45-93162a5a7afc| hdl-access = free}}</ref> It is a good source of nectar, and is the larval food plant of the [[marsh fritillary]],<ref>Howarth, T.G.1973. ''South's British Butterflies.'' p129.  Frederick Warne & Co. Ltd. {{ISBN|0-7232-1499-9}}</ref>  the eggs of which are laid in groups on the underside of the plant, and the narrow-bordered bee hawk-moth (''[[Hemaris tityus]]'').

The flowers are [[gall|galled]] by the [[gall midge]] ''[[Contarinia dipsacearum]]'', the leaves by the [[triozidae|triozid]] bug ''[[Trioza munda]]'', and the roots by the [[nematode]] ''[[Meloidogyne hapla]]''.<ref name="Ellis-2024"></ref>
[[File:Pathogens of Succisa pratensis Moench.png|thumb|An illustration showing some of the fungal and oomycetous pathogens that infect ''Succisa pratensis''.]]

The leaves are parasitized by the [[Chytridiomycota|chytrid fungus]] ''[[Synchytrium]] succisae'',<ref>Karling, J.S. 1964. ''Synchytrium''.Academic Press: New York.</ref> the [[powdery mildew]] ''[[Erysiphe knautiae]]'', the [[rust fungus]] ''[[Aecidium succisae]]'', and the [[leaf spot]] fungi ''[[Fusicladium consors]]'', ''[[Ramularia succisae]]'', ''[[Septoria succisicola]]'', and ''[[Septoria scabiosicola]]''.<ref name="Ellis-2024">{{cite web | vauthors=((Ellis, W. N.)) | year=2024 | title=''Succisa pratensis'' | website=bladmineerders.nl | url=https://bladmineerders.nl/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/eudicots/superasterids/asterids/campanulids/dipsacales/caprifoliaceae/dipsacoideae/succisa/succisa-pratensis/ | access-date=13 September 2024}}
</ref> The flowers are parasitised by the [[smut fungi|smut]] fungi ''[[Microbotryum succisae]]'' and ''[[Microbotryum flosculorum]]'', and the [[downy mildew]] ''[[Peronospora violacea]]''.<ref name="Ellis-2024"></ref>

==Management==
Its conservation is best promoted by an uneven patchwork of short and long vegetation by the end of the grazing period, between {{convert|8|and|25|cm|in|abbr=on}}. This can be achieved through low intensity grazing (also known as extensive grazing) using [[cattle]]. [[Sheep]] are not so good as they are more efficient at removing wild plants.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Bühler | first1=Christoph | last2=Schmid | first2=Bernhard | title=The influence of management regime and altitude on the population structure of ''Succisa pratensis'': implications for vegetation monitoring | journal=Journal of Applied Ecology | volume=38 | issue=4 | date=2001 | issn=0021-8901 | doi=10.1046/j.1365-2664.2001.00640.x | doi-access=free | pages=689–698 | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1046/j.1365-2664.2001.00640.x | access-date=2025-08-10}}</ref>

==In culture==
Allen and Hatfield<ref name=Allen>{{Cite book |last=Allen |first=D.E. |url=https://archive.org/details/medicinalplantsi00davi |title=Medicinal Plants in Folk Tradition |last2=Hatfield |first2=G. |year=2004 |isbn=0-88192-638-8}}</ref> describe how the truncated root of devil's-bit may have inspired belief in its magical properties, and led to its use as treatment for 'devil's bites' ([[scabies]]). They also claim it had a "well-founded reputation as an antiseptic" in Britain and the Isle of Man.

[[Nicholas Culpeper]] referred to devil's-bit as ''Marsus Diaboli'' (the devil's bite) and claimed that it was useful to take away swellings in the mouth. He wrote that there was not "a more present remedy in the world for those cold swellings in the neck which the vulgar call the 'almonds of the ears' than this herb bruised and applied to them".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Culpeper |first1=Nicholas |title=The Complete Herbal |date=1850 |publisher=Thomas Kelly |location=London |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/49513}}</ref> "Almonds of the ears" is an old name for the tonsils.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://johnsonsdictionaryonline.com/views/search.php?term=Tonsils| title=Tonsils |access-date=2025-10-10 |website=johnsonsdictionaryonline.com}}</ref>
